::: {.content-visible when-meta="draft"}

**Draft note (outline for the opening paragraph):**

- What this section delivers: evidence of overreporting, and its distribution, from production data alone, without audit data.
- Two steps: (1) a test for the presence of overreporting (this chapter); (2) deconvolution of its distribution (@sec-deconvolution).
- The key idea in one sentence: corporations do not overreport, so their materials share pins down the technology; any excess in unincorporated firms' reported share is overreporting plus noise.

:::

## Non-evaders {#sec-testing-nonevaders}

Because the firms' optimization decisions depend on the fiscal environment, the identification strategy should be motivated by the fiscal environment $\Gamma$. In particular, the identification strategy will be as good as how well we can tell apart a subset of firms that have the highest incentive to not evade. For example, in the case of Spain, the firms above the revenue LTU threshold. In the case of Colombia, the corporations (@sec-setting-jo).

**Assumption 1 (Non-evaders).** Based on the fiscal environment $\Gamma$, the researcher can identify a subset of firms $\theta_i\in\Theta^{NE}\subset \Theta$ that does not evade taxes by overreporting inputs.

For those firms, then $\mathbb{E}[u_{it}|\theta_i\in\Theta^{NE}]=0$.

In addition, I impose the following timing assumption.

**Assumption 2 (Independence).** The measurement error in output, $\varepsilon_{it}$, is independent of overreporting $u_{it}$ and of true materials $M_{it}$, with $\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_{it}]=0$.

::: {.content-visible when-meta="draft"}

**Draft note:** the approved paper states this as a timing assumption on an output shock ("firms choose overreporting before the output shock", citing @Gandhi2020, @Ackerberg2021, @Ackerberg2019). Following the supervisors, $\varepsilon$ is measurement error in output, not an output shock [@Gandhi2020], so independence is the classical measurement-error assumption and productivity is $\exp(\omega)$, not $\exp(\omega+\varepsilon)$. One sentence on why measurement error, and a contrast with GNR, belongs here or in @sec-model.

:::

## Identifying the output elasticity of materials {#sec-testing-beta}

Assume the production function is Cobb-Douglas, $M^{\beta}_{it}K_{it}^{\alpha_K}L_{it}^{\alpha_L}\exp(\omega_{it}+\varepsilon_{it})$. The econometrician observes output, capital, labour, and prices of intermediate inputs and output $\{Y_{it},K_{it},L_{it},\rho_t, P_t\}$, but she only observes overreported intermediate inputs, $M^*_{it}=M_{it}+e_{it}$. Let $u_{it}\equiv\ln(M^*_{it}/M_{it})=\ln(1+e_{it}/M_{it})$ denote the log overreporting ratio.

From the materials first-order condition (@eq-foc-m), by multiplying both sides by the intermediate inputs and dividing by the output, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
    \ln\left(\frac{\rho_t M_{it}}{P_{t}Y_{it}}\right) &=\ln\beta - \varepsilon_{it} \\
    \ln\left(\frac{\rho_t M^*_{it}}{P_{t}Y_{it}}\right) &=\ln\beta - \varepsilon_{it}+u_{it}
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-foc-cd}

where $Y_{it}$ is output as measured, with measurement error $\varepsilon_{it}$. We can use @eq-foc-cd and Assumptions 1 and 2 to recover the output elasticity of materials, $\beta$,

$$
    \ln\beta=\mathbb{E}\left[\ln\left(\frac{\rho_t M^*_{it}}{P_{t}Y_{it}}\right)\Bigg| \Theta^{NE}\right].
$$ {#eq-foc-cd-exp}

::: {.content-visible when-meta="draft"}

**Draft note:** the approved paper (`56-id-evasion.qmd`) carries GNR's constant $\mathcal E=E[\exp\varepsilon]$ (eq-id-E, eq-id-beta) because it treats $\varepsilon$ as an output shock. With measurement error there is no $\mathcal E$: the firm's FOC uses true output. Matches the code in use for ch. 6 and 8 (`first_stage_panel_me`, `big_E <- 1`). The test and the deconvolution only use $\ln\hat\beta=E[s\mid\text{corp}]$, so their results are the same under either convention.

:::

## The observed residual {#sec-testing-residual}

Having recovered the output elasticity of materials, $\beta$, for all firms, I can form the following variable using observed data.

$$
    \mathcal V_{it}\equiv\ln\left(\frac{\rho_t M^*_{it}}{P_{t}Y_{it}}\right)-\ln\beta=u_{it}-\varepsilon_{it}
$$ {#eq-ob-ev}

Tax evasion therefore can be recovered up to an independent random variable.

::: {.content-visible when-meta="draft"}

**Draft note (outline): why $u$, a ratio, and not the level $e$** (slides `700-deconvolving-evasion.qmd`, "I don't need $f_e$, actually"):

- Under Cobb-Douglas the firm's true materials are a share of revenue, so the wedge between $M^*$ and $M$ enters $\mathcal V$ only as $\ln(M^*/M)$, never as the level $e$.
- A ratio is adjusted for the firm's true input level, so it is comparable across firms of different sizes; a level $e$ would need normalizing anyway.
- @sec-deconvolution reports the overreporting ratio $e/M=\exp(u)-1$ directly.

:::

## Testing for overreporting {#sec-testing-test}

@eq-ob-ev suggests a way to test the presence of tax evasion through cost overreporting. Let $\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{V}_{it}]\equiv \mu_{\mathcal{V}}$ and define the null hypothesis as the absence of cost overreporting and the alternative hypothesis as the presence of cost overreporting. Consequently, to verify for the presence of tax evasion by overreporting, we can use a one-sided test where under the alternative hypothesis $H_1: \mu_{\mathcal{V}}>0$, and under the null, $H_0: \mu_{\mathcal{V}}\le0$.

I invert the test. For each industry, @tbl-evasion-test displays the estimated mean of $\mathcal V_{it}$ among unincorporated firms and the values of $\mu_{\mathcal V}$ in $[0,1]$ that the test does not reject at the 5 percent level, taking $\ln\hat\beta$ from corporations as the true value. The test detects overreporting where this set excludes zero. @sec-app-test-robustness reports a conservative version of the test and a bootstrap test that carries the sampling error of $\ln\hat\beta$.

::: {#tbl-evasion-test}
![](/tables/ch04-evasion-test.png)

Test for overreporting of materials by industry. Mean of $\mathcal V_{it}$ among unincorporated firms and 95 percent test-inversion region for its expectation (sharp test), with $\ln\beta$ estimated from corporations.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="draft"}

**Draft note (outline for the test design and results; replaces the old results paragraphs of `200-deconv.qmd`, whose industry counts come from an earlier table):**

- Design (2026-09-26, replaces the bootstrap): test inversion over $\mu_{\mathcal V}\in[0,1]$, with $\ln\hat\beta$ from corporations taken as the true value; moments (corporations: $s-\ln\hat D$; unincorporated firms: $s-\ln\hat D-\mu$), plant-clustered, centred covariance re-estimated at each candidate; sharp $\chi^2_1$ (the corporations' moment holds exactly at $\ln\hat D$), conservative $\chi^2_2$. Sample: log materials share net of sales taxes, juridical organization codes 6--9 excluded. The earlier bootstrap overstated significance: its resampling joined sampled plants back by plant only, so plants that switch legal form brought rows from the other group and the replicates were not centred on the estimate. The corrected bootstrap and the conservative test are in @sec-app-test-robustness.
- Results (@tbl-evasion-test), sharp test at 5 percent: the region excludes zero in 9 of 20 industries: 313 Beverages, 321 Textiles, 322 Wearing apparel, 324 Footwear, 331 Wood products, 342 Printing and publishing, 369 Non-metallic minerals, and, at the margin (lower ends 0.001 and 0.002), 351 Industrial chemicals and 352 Other chemicals. At 1 percent: the first seven. Conservative test at 5 percent: the same seven (351 and 352 no longer reject).
- Why this is not cherry-picking (three devices, all using every industry tested):
  - Ranking fixed before the test: four of the five largest industries by output (313, 321, 351, 352; not 311), from the revenue ranking (`Code/Thesis/ch03-industry-stats.R`; the ch. 3 industry tables were cut 2026-09-26, so cite the ranking here if this argument stays). Two of the four (351, 352) are marginal.
  - Size-weighted (nominal gross output 1981--91, codes 6--9 excluded; recomputed 2026-09-26, the earlier figures could not be reproduced exactly): the 20 industries tested produce 89.9 percent of manufacturing output; the 9 with evidence produce 46.0 percent of the tested output, 41.3 percent of all manufacturing output. At 1 percent (7 industries): 29.4 and 26.4 percent.
  - Multiple testing: with 20 tests at 5 percent, about one rejection is expected by chance if no industry overreports; nine or more has probability $2\times10^{-7}$ (binomial; industry samples are separate).
- The deconvolution uses a rule fixed before seeing magnitudes: the industries whose 99 percent sharp region excludes zero (seven).
- Consistent with incentives: little or no evidence in industries whose products are exempt from the sales tax (311, 312, 382, 384); 311 no longer rejects once codes 6--9 are excluded.
- Empty regions (323 Leather, 356 Plastics, 384 Transport equipment): the mean of $\mathcal V$ is negative, so every $\mu\ge0$ is rejected.
- Industries where zero is not rejected: 311, 312, 332, 341, 381, 382, 383, 390. For these and for the empty regions, state only that the result is inconclusive, and that anyone interested in a particular industry should investigate whether the identifying assumptions hold there before drawing conclusions. Do not speculate about which assumption fails (Hans, 2026-09-24).

**Draft note (outline): what the test needs, and what it does not.** Stated in PLAN.md §10.

- Valid for any detection function and evasion cost with $q(0,Z)=0$ and $\kappa(0,Z)=0$: at $e=0$ the evasion terms of profit vanish, so a non-evader's materials FOC is the standard one.
- Technology need not be Cobb-Douglas, only common within the industry: under the null the share residual is $-\varepsilon$ for every firm.
- The direction is always overreporting: with general technology the residual is $[u-(\ln D(M^*)-\ln D(M))]-\varepsilon$, and the bracket is positive because $d\ln D/d\ln M<1$ when $D>0$ and $Y_{MM}\le0$; and no firm gains by underreporting deductible costs.
- Maths checked (2026-09-25, corrected with Hans the same night). (i) $\kappa(0,Z)=0$ for all $Z$ is sufficient, including $Z=M$: every $q$ term in profit is multiplied by $e$, so at $e=0$ it and its $M$-derivative vanish even if $\partial q/\partial M\neq0$, and $\partial\kappa(0,M)/\partial M=0$. Under the null no firm's materials FOC is distorted, so the test's size is exact and a rejection means $e>0$ somewhere. $\partial q/\partial M\neq0$ or $\partial\kappa/\partial M\neq0$ can only distort evaders' true materials under the alternative (power), never produce a false rejection. (ii) Direction: adding and subtracting true materials, $\ln(\rho M^*/PY)-\ln D(K,L,M^*)=[u-(\ln D(M^*)-\ln D(M))]-\varepsilon$, with $D=MG_M/G$ and $d\ln D/d\ln M=1+MG_{MM}/G_M-D<1$ when $G_{MM}\le0$, $D>0$; so the bracket is positive whenever $e>0$, and it is $-\varepsilon$ exactly under the null. (iii) Technology: holds for any parametric common technology (e.g. translog), estimating its parameters on corporations and evaluating $D$ at each firm's own reported inputs; the functional form carries the extrapolation, so no input overlap between corporations and unincorporated firms is needed (overlap would matter only for a nonparametric $D$). The share of a flexible, non-deductible input (labour) helps pin down $D$ beyond Cobb-Douglas (`56-id-evasion.qmd`, two flexible inputs). The test as run is the Cobb-Douglas case (one $\ln\hat\beta$ per industry).
- Contrast with deconvolution (@sec-deconvolution draft note): deconvolution also needs $\partial q/\partial M=\partial\kappa/\partial M=0$ and a constant output elasticity of materials; the test needs neither.

:::
